papers.title: High-Performance All-Atom Continuous Constant-pH Molecular Dynamics and Native Asynchronous Replica Exchange in Amber
papers.abstract: Conformational dynamics of biomolecules, including proteins and nucleic acids, are often coupled to changes in protonation states. All-atom particle-mesh Ewald continuous constant-pH molecular dynamics (PME-CpHMD) enables proton-coupled dynamics, but its routine use has been limited by computational cost. Here we report a second-generation CUDA implementation of PME-CpHMD in Amber, in which the CpHMD-specific nonbonded corrections are evaluated in a separate kernel. Across protein systems ranging from 45 to 1,338 residues, the new implementation increases throughput by 1.5-2 fold relative to the previous fused-kernel implementation and limits the overhead relative to conventional MD to 12-18%. We also implemented the asynchronous pH replica-exchange (pH-REX) algorithm natively in pmemd.cuda.MPI, allowing simulations to run on fewer GPUs than replicas without the overhead of the previous Python wrapper. Furthermore, we derived CpHMD titration parameters for all six titratable residue types (Asp, Glu, His, Cys, Tyr, and Lys) for use with three protein force fields: CHARMM c22/CMAP, Amber ff14sb and ff19sb. The new implementations and parameterization were validated using pKa calculations of model peptides and hen egg white lysozyme (HEWL). The HEWL simulations revealed force-field-specific limitations, including overestimation of the pKa downshift 20 of H15 and sensitivity of the proton donor assignment in coupled E35/D52 dyad. Comparison with our previous work and the PME-CpHMD simulations in GROMACS with the CHARMM c36m force field demonstrated the robustness and sampling efficiency of pH-REX PME-CpHMD simulations. The new implementation provides a foundation for routine all-atom constant-pH simulations in Amber. The analysis highlights the need for continued development of protein force fields to more accurately balance intramolecular electrostatics and solvation of charged residues.

papers.title: A unique sixth-order reversible assembly of hexameric mimetic nucleic acid
papers.abstract: Complementary dipeptides bearing the non-canonical nucleobases melamine and cyanuric acid (alpha DPNA) assemble into a cylindrical hexameric structure containing a stacked heterocyclic core with its beta-sheet peptide backbones on the surface. Circular dichroism spectroscopy and singular-value decomposition show that the evolution of CD spectra after mixing equimolar strands is an apparent two-state process, accounted for by only the spectra of free strands and the assembled hexamer, with no detectable intermediates. Equilibrium measurements reveal a highly cooperative, enthalpically driven assembly with a molecularity of 6.2 +/- 0.2 and an association constant of (2.3 +/- 0.2)X10^22 " " M^(-5). Over total strand concentrations of 20 to 100 micromolar, the assembly progress curves are described by an apparent reversible sixth-order macroscopic rate law. This deceptively simple behavior cannot represent an elementary six-strand collision. The apparent forward rate constant has a negative activation energy, showing that the observed rate law masks additional steps in the assembly reaction. A minimal model in which strand pre-isomerization precedes hexamer formation restores a physically reasonable positive activation energy while retaining the observed two-state CD behavior. Constrained simulations further show that a sequential pathway with low-population, spectroscopically silent, intermediates can give rise to the same deceptively simple sixth-order progress curve. These results provide an unusual example of highly cooperative hexamer formation and show how a simple high-order macroscopic rate law can conceal a more complex microscopic assembly mechanism. The thermodynamics and kinetics provide insights into how and why the hexamer assembles, offering some design principles for supramolecular assemblies in water.

papers.title: Binary Patterning as a Probe of Protein Language Model Representations
papers.abstract: Do protein language models (pLMs) encode the physical rules that govern protein folding? The four-helix bundle provides a classic test case because binary patterning, the ordered placement of polar and nonpolar residues along an amphipathic -helix, is sufficient to generate folded proteins with high probability. Here, we ask whether ESM2 captures the sequence grammar underlying this design strategy. Libraries of synthetic sequences constrained only by binary patterning were predicted by ESMFold to form four-helix bundles. Predicted helicity, compactness, and topological diversity changed with sequence length in the same direction as experimentally characterized libraries, although the model did not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings revealed representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extending the analysis to all 128 heptad binary patterns produced a jellyfish-shaped manifold in which hydrophobic composition formed the dominant axis, while paired components encoded pattern phase. Manifold geometry depended on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapsed when amino acids were assigned to arbitrary categories. ESM2 therefore combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information. More broadly, synthetic sequence libraries provide experimentally grounded probes of protein language model representations and their relationship to protein biophysics.

papers.title: Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
papers.abstract: Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.

papers.title: Computational Insights into How Structural Changes in the Hydrophobic Region of ALS-Linked Mutant SOD1 (G93A) Activate Fluctuations of the Electrostatic Loop: Implications for Aggregation
papers.abstract: Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD1) is an essential antioxidant enzyme that converts superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. On the other hand, mutations in SOD1 cause familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (fALS), and these mutant forms tend to aggregate. Our previous research has shown that residue I35, located in a hydrophobic region, plays a critical role in the intracellular aggregation of SOD1. Furthermore, introducing an additional I35S mutation suppressed aggregate formation and eye degeneration in a Drosophila model caused by ALS-linked mutant SOD1. However, the molecular mechanism linking structural changes induced by ALS mutations to aggregation, and how the compensatory I35S mutation suppresses this aggregation, remain unclear. To elucidate the relationship between structural changes and aggregation, molecular dynamics simulations were performed on three types of SOD1 monomers: wild type (WT), G93A (an fALS mutant), and the G93A/I35S double mutant. In WT, the metal-binding loop (loop IV) exhibited slightly larger fluctuations, whereas in G93A, the electrostatic loop (loop VII) fluctuates significantly more. Detailed analysis revealed that the G93A mutation shifts the hydrogen-bonding partner of the 93rd residue from L38 in WT to G37 in G93A. This change destabilizes the V119-L144 hydrogen bond, thereby enhancing fluctuations in {beta}-strand 8 and the electrostatic loop. Notably, the I35S mutation in the G93A background restores the WT-like packing of the hydrophobic core and reestablishes the V119-L144 hydrogen bond, reducing the abnormal electrostatic loop fluctuations. These findings provide a mechanistic link between a single-point mutation and conformational changes involved in SOD1 aggregation. Our results also suggest that targeting the hydrophobic region may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for SOD1-linked fALS.

papers.title: Cochlear wave dispersion reveals partition micromechanics
papers.abstract: Cochlear traveling waves are a fundamental aspect of mammalian hearing, enabling frequency selectivity. However, incorporating micromechanical interactions between the cells, membranes, and fluids that comprise the cochlear partition presents a challenge when accounting for this selectivity and other macro-scale response properties. The traveling wave can be characterized by its dispersion, which is the relationship between its wavenumber and frequency. One objective was to investigate how organ of Corti structural components influence wave dispersion. To achieve this, we adapted a conventional three-dimensional tapered cochlear box model by incrementally adding morphological characteristics that constitute the partition. Initially a flexible plate, the partition transformed to incorporate a tectorial membrane and inner spiral sulcus. Our secondary objective was to predict the dispersion for each variation using a reduced-length model (slice model). We observed that stiffness and the optimal frequency increased across variations, while wave dispersion remained unchanged relative to the optimal frequency. We also discovered that eigenfrequency analysis, using Floquet boundary conditions, accurately predicted the dispersion for each variation and revealed the existence of other propagating waves including a tectorial membrane transverse mode. These results underscore the significance of analyzing cochlear wave propagation from capturing macromechanical response properties thereby facilitating investigations of micromechanical interactions in reduced-length models.

papers.title: Overlap of competing voices may mask attentional effects on speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions
papers.abstract: Whether selective auditory attention modulates the cochlear amplifier through the medial olivocochlear system remains debated. Using speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), elicited by waveforms that follow the harmonics of natural speech, we previously found that selectively attending one of two competing talkers reduced the emissions related to the resolved harmonics of the female voice. Here, we attempted to reproduce this effect in a design that separated different frequency regimes and harmonic resolvability. Forty-four participants attended one of two competing talkers, a female and a male voice, presented to one ear, while speech-like DPOAEs related to both voices were recorded from the other ear. Stimuli were derived from resolved and unresolved harmonics in a low-frequency (up to 1.5 kHz) and a transitional (1.5 to 4 kHz) regime, which required pitch-shifting both voices so that their fundamental frequencies were much closer to each other than in the original study. Speech-like DPOAEs emerged for most stimulus types, although they were weak for some and absent for one. Their amplitude, however, did not depend on attention for any stimulus type. Further time-domain metrics showed only isolated attentional effects of opposite direction for two stimulus types, and a frequency-domain metric showed none. A cochlear excitation model suggests that, due to the closely spaced fundamental frequencies of the two voices, the emissions most comparable to the original study presumably arose at cochlear locations shared by both voices, where attention would modulate both voices alike.

papers.title: Lipid Scrambling Amplifies Plasma Membrane Undulations via Anti-Registered Domains Stabilized by Long-Chain Sphingomyelin
papers.abstract: Lipid scrambling, which dissipates the transbilayer lipid asymmetry of plasma membranes (PMs), plays an essential role in various large-scale membrane remodeling processes. Although lipid domains have been implicated in these processes, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, owing to the lack of a molecular-level picture of how lipid scrambling reorganizes these domains. Here, using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of asymmetric and fully scrambled PM models, we show that lipid scrambling markedly enhances membrane undulations. We identify two key features of the domain organization underlying this enhancement in the scrambled PM: domain anti-registration, which couples to membrane curvature through a mismatch in preferred curvature between the two leaflets, and scrambling-induced domain enlargement, which permits this curvature to extend over large length scales. Simulations with different sphingomyelin (SM) compositions demonstrate that long-chain SMs stabilize anti-registered domains and the associated membrane curvature. Together, these results suggest a physical mechanism by which lipid scrambling primes the PM for remodeling through the reorganization of lipid domains, with long-chain SMs playing a key role. We also find that the interleaflet domain organization of the scrambled PM model depends strongly on system size, shifting from anti-registration to registration as the simulation box is reduced, and we discuss the origin of this finite-size effect.

papers.title: DNA Sequence Differentially Modulates Histone Core and Tail Interactions in Canonical and Centromeric Nucleosomes
papers.abstract: Human centromeric chromatin is a specialized chromatin domain characterized by CENP-A-containing nucleosomes interspersed with canonical histone H3 nucleosomes. It is assembled on tandem repeats of -satellite DNA and defines centromere identity. How histone variant identity and DNA sequence jointly shape nucleosome structure and histone-DNA interactions that underpin centromeric chromatin formation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the structural plasticity of the histone core and nucleosomal DNA, histone tail dynamics and DNA-sequence dependent changes for canonical (H3) and centromeric (CENP-A) nucleosomes using the SIRAH coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) simulations. Nucleosomes containing -satellite positioning sequence (ASP) and Widom 601 DNA sequence are systematically analyzed and compared. Our simulations reveal that the centromeric nucleosome exhibits a more stable histone core with lower structural plasticity and the histone tails engage DNA differently with an overall reduction in the histone-DNA contacts compared to the canonical nucleosome. Further investigation of CENP-N binding to the CENP-A nucleosome demonstrates substantial modulation of nucleosomal DNA dynamics and histone-DNA interactions. Replacing the ASP DNA sequence with the Widom 601 sequence preserves the stability of both types of the histone core while markedly altering histone-tail dynamics. The conformational dynamics of canonical nucleosomes is more strongly affected by the Widom 601 DNA sequence than those of their centromeric counterparts. However, CENP-N binding induces more spatially extensive changes in DNA geometry in Widom 601 than in ASP DNA. Our findings suggest that DNA sequence and histone composition have residue-level differences translating into distinct nucleosome dynamics, which could be among the determinants governing the structural and dynamic properties of centromeric chromatin and its biological function.

papers.title: Evaluating speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions: a comparison of time- and frequency-domain metrics across three datasets
papers.abstract: Speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) allow cochlear activity to be measured during the perception of natural, continuous speech and have been used to study attentional effects in the cochlea. The technique is still young, however, and existing studies differ in stimulus design and in the metric used to quantify the emissions, which makes their results difficult to compare. Here, we reanalysed three existing datasets (106 participants, 14 stimulus types) with a common pipeline. We compared six metrics: the band power of the recording, the magnitude-squared coherence (MSC) between the recording and a DPOAE template, and four metrics derived from their complex cross-correlation, namely peak magnitude, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), peak area and peak width. A separability index quantified how well each metric separated in-ear recordings from out-of-ear control recordings without emissions. Band power, MSC and SNR separated best, with mean separability indices of about 0.9, whereas the peak magnitude performed worst and was inverted for half of the stimulus types. Since band power does not require a DPOAE template, it serves as a sanity check of the setup rather than as evidence for an emission. The MSC was insensitive to the latency of the emission but well suited for comparisons across stimuli, whereas the cross-correlation additionally provided the latency. The emissions differed significantly between the stimulus types of the three datasets, and those below about 700 Hz were measured least reliably. We derive practical recommendations for the analysis and stimulus design of future experiments.

papers.title: Torque generation and regulation in the flagellar motor of Campylobacter jejuni differ from those of model organisms
papers.abstract: The bacterial flagellar motor is a rotary nanomachine that powers motility by driving the rotation of a helical filament. Most of our mechanistic understanding of this motor derives from studies of model organisms, particularly Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, yet recent structural work has revealed substantial architectural diversity, raising questions about the universality of established biophysical models. Here, we present the first single-motor measurements of torque output and stator dynamics in Campylobacter jejuni, a species with a structurally elaborate motor adapted for motility in high-viscosity environments. The C.~jejuni motor generates an exceptionally high stall torque (~3600~pN{middle dot}nm) and, rather than the biphasic torque--speed relationship characteristic of model systems, exhibits an approximately linear decline in torque with increasing speed over the measured range. Time-resolved measurements reveal discrete speed changes, indicating that the stator output remains dynamic despite the presence of a scaffolded stator ring. The inferred number of active stator units averaged 11{+/-}4, below the 17-unit complement observed structurally, and showed no clear dependence on viscous load despite substantial motor-to-motor heterogeneity. Following transient collapse of the proton motive force, motor activity recovers rapidly, consistent with reversible activation of pre-associated stator units. Together, these findings reveal a distinct mode of flagellar motor operation, consistent with dynamic regulation of a preassembled stator ring rather than regulation through physical stator exchange, and show that the canonical behavior defined in model organisms is not universal.

papers.title: Interplay of diffusive and active motion governs cohesin extrusion and CTCF barrier function
papers.abstract: Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion constitutes a crucial process for the regulation of chromosome folding and gene expression. A rapidly-growing body of in vitro experiments suggests that cohesin molecular motor activity is finely modulated by both chemical and mechanical cues, whose interplay holds important implications in living cells for development and disease. Yet, biophysical models capable of accurately and efficiently capturing the breadth of reported cohesin behaviors, along with their impacts on DNA spatio-temporal organisation, remain lacking. Here, building on multiple experimental observations of single-cohesin dynamics, we introduce a mesoscale description of cohesin based on the general framework of jump-diffusion processes. We show that the finite stall force of cohesin naturally emerges from the conjunction of active, directional extrusion moves with passive, stochastic drift. The tension-dependent competition between these two orthogonal modes of motion gives rise to highly-heterogeneous cohesin kinetics featuring extrusion, translocation, and loop slipping phases, as observed in vitro. These behaviors are predicted to depend sensitively on both buffer composition and nucleosomal content, reconciling the surprising variability of cohesin kinetics reported across experimental conditions. This jump-diffusion model (JDM) is fully parametrized using available single-molecule measurements and bridges the timescale gap between microscopic stepping events and cohesin regulator association, thus providing mechanistic insights into how CTCF impedes extrusion. Hence, the JDM quantitatively describes force-dependent extrusion in both DNA curtain assays in vitro and in the context of native chromatin for genome folding predictions in nucleo, bridging these previously disparate contexts under a unified numerical and theoretical formalism.

papers.title: Filament mechanics and turnover organize dynamic load bearing structures in a cellular-scale model of the actomyosin cortex
papers.abstract: The actomyosin cortex controls cell shape and movement by generating and transmitting contractile forces. Its actin filament (AF) network adopts diverse spatial organizations, while spatially biased contractility drives cortical flow that transports components and reorganizes the network. However, how turnover and spatial redistribution organize and maintain tension-bearing structures in a dynamic steady state, and how localized contractility reorganizes them through flow, remain unclear. We developed a cellular-scale discrete model of the actomyosin cortex representing AFs, cross-linkers, and myosin minifilaments. Local surface stress was reconstructed from discrete-element internal forces based on continuum mechanics. We related cortical tension to component abundance, tensile deformation, AF orientation, turnover, and network connectivity, and compared different AF disassembly, relocation, and myosin-localization mechanisms. Simulations produced a heterogeneous, network-like distribution of local cortical tension. Tensile energy per element correlated more strongly with local tension than component abundance, with the strongest correlation for AFs. Highly stretched AFs preferentially occurred in high-tension regions and aligned with the first-principal-tension orientation, indicating anisotropic load-bearing pathways. Despite continuous component replacement and reorganization of local tension patterns, global AF-network connectivity and cell-scale cortical tension were maintained. The characteristic time of tension-pattern reorganization was closest to the persistence time of myosin, suggesting an association between myosin dynamics and rapid force redistribution. AF relocation to low-density regions replenished spatial gaps, whereas bending-dependent disassembly limited the accumulation of strongly deformed AFs. Direct myosin localization and AF accumulation produced comparable equatorward cortical flows but differed in the spatial organization of the tension-bearing network. Collectively, these results demonstrate that cellular-scale cortical tension is organized not only by component abundance but also by filament-scale mechanical loading, AF orientation, and network connectivity.

papers.title: Theory of large-bead AFM compression of pressurized rod-shaped bacteria
papers.abstract: Motivated by our atomic force microscopy (AFM) experiments measuring turgor pressure in living bacteria, we develop a theoretical description of pressurized spherocylindrical cells compressed by spherical probes whose radius greatly exceeds the cell radius. In this global-loading regime, the mechanical response is governed primarily by cell geometry and turgor pressure, while the elastic properties of the cell envelope enter as higher-order corrections. The strong confinement imposed by the probe drives water efflux from the cytoplasm, thereby increasing the turgor pressure. We present a theoretical framework for determining bacterial turgor pressure from AFM force--displacement curves, accounting for cell geometry and probe dimensions. Combining numerical simulations with analytical theory, we show that the mechanical response can be approximated in terms of cylindrical and hemispherical contributions. The leading-order force--displacement dependency is captured by an analytical description derived in the large-aspect-ratio limit, where the mechanics reduce to a tension-dominated cross-sectional problem. Finite cell aspect ratio and probe curvature are incorporated through geometric renormalizations. The resulting framework provides a quantitative basis for extracting bacterial turgor pressure from AFM measurements while simultaneously predicting cell deformation geometry.

papers.title: Inferring chromatin looping interactions from microscopy-based measurements: opportunities and pitfalls
papers.abstract: Chromatin looping plays essential roles in several nuclear processes and live-cell microscopy has become a key method for studying how chromatin loops behave in time. Extracting dynamical parameters including looping probability, lifetime, and search time from live-imaging data requires inferring looping events from noisy 3D distance trajectories. By analyzing polymer simulation data with known ground truth, we show that with realistic localization precision, the common method of simple thresholding on 3D distance measurements can result in severe misestimation of looping probability, lifetime, and search time. We use simple statistical considerations to show that inference from simple thresholding becomes infeasible when localization error is comparable to the size of the interaction to be studied. Finally, we demonstrate how noise-aware methods can be used to estimate looping parameters more accurately in these regimes.

papers.title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
papers.abstract: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.

papers.title: Catalytic domain-lipid interactions negatively regulate RhoA signaling by modulating conformational dynamics
papers.abstract: RhoA belongs to the Ras superfamily of small GTPases, regulates cytoskeletal actin organization and cell motility, and is implicated in cancer metastasis and neurodegenerative diseases. It is predominantly anchored to the cytosolic side of the plasma membrane (PM) via its prenylated C-terminus, but little is known about its PM organization, dynamics, and lipid interactions. In this work, we used extensive atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and simulations-guided experiments to study the molecular details and functional consequences of RhoA membrane targeting, interactions and dynamics. We found that both GDP- and GTP-bound RhoA adopt a well-defined, stable membrane organization and binding mode irrespective of initial conditions and bilayer lipid composition. RhoA membrane organization is determined by hydrophobic interaction of the prenylated C-terminus with the membrane, and a previously unknown, critical role of electrostatic interactions between cationic residues on the G-domain and N-terminus with anionic lipids in the PM. N-terminal interactions are mediated by a polybasic patch including residues R5, K6, and K7, and substitution of these residues with Ala increased RhoA-mediated F-actin accumulation and effector activation in cells. MD simulations suggest that the triple mutant retains the global membrane organization of wild type RhoA but alters key protein-lipid interactions. Specifically, we observe a loss of cooperative lipid engagement involving the polybasic patch and Switch II residues with amine-bearing lipids, and a rerouting of intra-protein dynamic networks that primes Switch I for effector recognition. These results suggest that the membrane serves not just as a scaffold but also as an allosteric partner of RhoA to fine-tune intra-protein dynamics in a functionally relevant manner.

papers.title: Where the magnet sits sets the sign of the scaling law: membrane-anchored versus intracellular magnetic actuation of cells
papers.abstract: Magnetic nanoparticles apply mechanical force to cells in two incompatible geometries: anchored to the plasma membrane, where a rotating field twists a surface-bound cap, and internalized into lysosomes, where an assembled rod stirs the organelle lumen. They are treated as interchangeable, and the choice is made on synthetic convenience. They obey opposite design rules. Treated analytically at matched single-cell magnetic moment, the step-out frequency of an intracellular rod falls with assembly size while that of a membrane cap rises linearly; the scaling exponents have opposite sign and the curves cross at 184 particles and 4.04 Hz, inside the window in which published experiments operate. The cap tension resultant reduces to an identity in which cell radius cancels, leaving magnetic texture as the decisive design variable: a field-oriented cap reaches 2.69 mN m-1, the same particles with random easy axes reach 0.0033 mN m-1, and a superparamagnetic cap transmits no torque at all. The model reproduces four published measurements with no fitted parameters. One disagrees: our intralysosomal wall shear stress is 33 to 81 times below the published value while reproducing every structural feature of it. The model yields two zero-predictions that one experiment would falsify.

papers.title: Binding mechanisms of therapeutic antibodies to human claudin-18.2
papers.abstract: Claudin-18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a tight junction component with highly restricted expression in the paracellular space of nonmalignant gastric epithelial cells. It becomes accessible on tumor cell surface during malignant transformation, making CLDN18.2 an attractive target for targeted therapies against gastric cancer. Recently, zolbetuximab has become the first FDA-approved monoclonal antibody that targets CLDN18.2 in advanced gastric cancer, and others like osemitamab have entered phase 3 clinical trials. However, the high-resolution structure of CLDN18.2 is lacking, and how CLDN18.2 is recognized by therapeutic antibodies remains undefined. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human claudin-18.2 (hCLDN18.2) in complex with the Fab fragments of zolbetuximab and osemitamab, revealing the structure of hCLDN18.2 and its binding mechanism to the therapeutic antibodies. Further analyses reveal that three residues in the first extracellular loop of hCLDN18.2 that are different from human claudin-18.1 (hCLDN18.1) play a critical role in antibody binding. Our data elucidate the structural basis for selective binding of therapeutic antibodies to hCLDN18.2, which should aid rational design of next-generation immunotherapies targeting hCLDN18.2.

papers.title: Structural relationships between the SLC12 cotransporter C-terminal domain, universal stress proteins and adenylating enzymes
papers.abstract: Several SLC12 cotransporters bind ATP in a cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD). We analysed 16,192 CTD-containing SLC12 sequences and compared 42,845 representative structures to examine the relationship between this nucleotide site, universal stress proteins (USPs) and adenylating enzymes. In phosphorylated NKCC1, D891 and D927 lie near the ATP phosphate chain, while R801 and K889 form a basic phosphate-binding clamp. NKCC1 retains this arrangement, whereas KCC paralogs replace or lose several corresponding groups. In structural comparisons with USP and adenylating-enzyme references, both CTD lobes score between universal stress proteins and EC-annotated domains, and the two lobes form separate lineages that include bacterial transporters. Lobe-specific and nucleotide-frame comparisons place ATP in the corresponding structural region used for -phosphate chemistry by catalytic members of this fold. Published work on UspG provides a precedent for protein-bound AMP in a natural USP. In the examined SLC12 structures and USP models, candidate protein hydroxyls lack an in-line geometry for attack at ATP P. Protein adenylation would require a change in protein or nucleotide geometry, or a different acceptor. These results define a structural basis for testing conditional protein adenylation at SLC12 nucleotide sites. The required evidence is a covalent protein-AMP adduct, identification of its acceptor and measurement of the expected pyrophosphate coproduct, with soluble nucleotide analysis to distinguish accompanying ATP reactions.

papers.title: Beyond Sequence and Structure: Pretraining PLMs on Continuous Biophysical Fields
papers.abstract: We introduce the Biophysical Transformer, a protein language model that adds continuous biophysical fields as a third pretraining signal beside sequence and structure. A Poisson-Boltzmann solver computes the electrostatic potential around each three-residue token, and the model learns to predict it from sequence alone. A rotationally invariant spherical-harmonic descriptor serves as the loss target, eliminating the need for frame alignment during training and for coordinates at inference. Against a matched, one-flag control on the FLIP Meltome thermostability benchmark, the field objective raises Spearman correlation on every trained head of both human splits.The gain on human survives residualizing dipeptide composition under two architecturally different readouts and survives removing the test proteins that overlap the pretraining corpus. No effect survives on the organism-mixed split. At 1.1M parameters, both the Biophysical Transformer and its sequence-only control exceed FLIP's one-hot CNN and untrained-ESM baselines on every split. All results rest on a single pretraining run per arm,and the current design does not separate field content from generic regularization.

papers.title: Design of colipids with controlled lateral distance of head group moieties for targeting strategies in the field of lipid-based nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles and liposomes are nanoparticle drug formulations which are firmly established in clinics. In order to expand their application and improve efficacy, surface modifications can be a key strategy, especially for cell specific targeting. Targeting can be achieved by integrating ligand functionalized lipids or lipidoids on the nanoparticle surface. In this case, not solely the targeting ligand itself, but also the structure of the whole targeting lipid/lipidoid can affect the interaction of the targeting ligand with the binding motive on cells. Especially, distal spacer structures between lipid anchor and ligand unit, often composed of polyethylene glycol chains, provide a certain distance of the ligand from the nanoparticle surface. A concept which is currently neglected is the control of the lateral distance between ligand structures on the nanoparticle. Herein we investigated the possibility to design lipidoids with a lateral spacer composed of polyethylene glycol units. We synthesized and characterized different lipidoids which provide a primary amine in the head group for possible ligand coupling. In our model lipidoids the head groups were functionalized with a paramagnetic probe to apply electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) methods for the characterization of the lipidoid interaction with model nanoparticles, in our case liposomes. Continuous wave EPR was used to study the efficiency of the novel lipidoids to integrate into lipid bilayers of model liposomes, which was shown to depend on lipidoid structure and liposome composition. Furthermore, using double electron-electron resonance (DEER), we observed lipidoid conformational changes occurring upon integration into liposomes.

papers.title: An auditable harness for biomolecular dynamics simulations by AI agents
papers.abstract: AI agents now generate biological hypotheses faster than they can be tested. Hypotheses stated at the atomic level can be examined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For new questions without a reference, trust in an agent-run simulation rests on a tool-written process record, not the agent's account. Existing MD agents leave this record to the language model. Here we present MDClaw, a harness whose validating tools and directed acyclic graph (DAG) check stages before execution and record every simulation stage. On MDDataBench, which grades outputs against deposited simulations, four open-weight models with MDClaw passed all three runs on 81-100% of 31 test systems. The DAG complements this outcome check. An ablation without the DAG revealed 11 successful runs that had skipped minimization or equilibration, or simulated a different structure. MDClaw carried questions from human and AI scientists through simulation to trajectories traceable to their inputs and settings.

papers.title: Quantifying electro-osmotic flow in mutant MspA nanopores
papers.abstract: Nanopores have emerged as a powerful tool for single-molecule sensing and sequencing. In a typical nanopore experiment, a charged analyte such as DNA is driven through the pore by an electrophoretic force generated by the applied electric field. This can be problematic, however, when analytes such as proteins carry mixed charges. An alternative driving force can be from electro-osmotic flow (EOF), the water flow that arises from an asymmetric migration of cations and anions through the nanopore. However, despite much recent interest, there is no straightforward experimental method to quantify EOF in nanopores. Here, we trap a dipolar peptide in an MspA nanopore, where studying its escape rate versus voltage allows us to extract the work done by the EOF in various MspA mutants and wildtype MspA compared to a M2-MspA reference. For the 30 amino acid model peptide, this yields values of ~5.6-16.7 kBT for the work done by the EOF at 80 mV. Finite-element simulations confirm the trends observed in the experiments. Charged mutations close to the nanopore's constriction site are found to produce the highest EOF. Our novel method provides a quantitative metric of the EOF in nanopores, opening up its study and broad use in future nanopore sequencing and sensing applications.

papers.title: Formation of perinuclear actin structures is driven by mechanosensitivity of actin polymerization
papers.abstract: Actin filaments are one of the most dynamic components of the cytoskeleton. Their fast polymerization, particularly in regions around the nucleus, allows the cell to react quickly and efficiently to external mechanical stimuli by controling nucleus morphology and position, thereby influencing the chromatin organization and gene transcription. While the biochemical mechanisms of actin polymerization are well known, the question why polymerization happens most prominently in the perinuclear region has so far remained elusive. Here, we develop a computational model for actin network formation whose key ingredients are: (i) a fully resolved orientational distribution of the local filaments, (ii) a strain-dependent depolymerization rate and (iii) active stress generation by actomyosin motors. With only these ingredients and without any ad-hoc assumptions on the spatial distribution of signaling molecules, our physics-based model explains the formation of perinuclear actin structures after mechanical stimulation as observed experimentally. In addition, our model also provides some insight into the role actin plays in positioning the nucleus, as it predicts the occurrence of a re-centering force when the cell nucleus is displaced, in quantitative agreement with experimental observations.

papers.title: Dynamical Fingerprints of Rare-Event Transitions from Transition Corridors
papers.abstract: Rare transitions are central in science, yet their mechanisms are obscured by the high dimensionality of complex dynamics, a challenge particularly pronounced in biomolecules where rare conformational transitions underlie functional processes. A transition-conditioned dynamical fingerprint is introduced for a rare (A mathbin{text{--}} B) event, in which the transition-relevant subset is targeted rather than a global decomposition and the problem is treated dynamically. Within a selected transition corridor, barrier-crossing motion is extracted and microscopic players are ranked through a corridor-conditioned informativeness measure, after which the highest-ranked players are subjected to intervention tests of their transition leverage using the REST2 scaling scheme, metadynamics, and targeted mutation. Across three benchmark proteins, targeting these players facilitates basin-to-basin transitions while maintaining high fidelity to the prescribed transition corridor, providing handles for mechanistic analysis, enhanced sampling, control, and design.

papers.title: Unavoidable Disasters: the Hsp70 Chaperone Can Only Prevent Aggregation Over a Limited Time Span
papers.abstract: Cells must attain and maintain proper protein folding and avoid aggregation: this is a pervasive challenge across all domains of life. Molecular chaperones are central to this process, acting through mechanisms shaped by the free-energy landscapes of their client proteins. The impact of chaperones on client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic characteristics, however, remains poorly characterized. Here, we develop the CHAMPION70 computational model to perform kinetic simulations on the E. Coli Hsp70 chaperone system in the presence of client-protein folding and aggregation. Experimentally determined folding/unfolding/aggregation rate constants are taken into account. In the case of weakly aggregation-prone clients, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 prevents aggregation only over timescales approaching the average human lifespan (79 years). For strongly aggregation-prone clients, however, aggregation inevitably occurs starting from a few minutes, even at higher-than-physiological Hsp70 concentrations. Thus, the Hsp70 chaperone system merely delays, yet surprisingly does not eliminate, the onset of aggregation. Further, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 most effectively retards the aggregation of slow-folding, thermodynamically stable clients. In contrast, thermodynamically unstable clients remain engaged with Hsp70 for prolonged periods even when aggregation propensity is low, thereby consuming chaperone capacity and reducing the extent of productive folding. This outcome suggests that condensate formation by proteins containing disordered regions may serve to mitigate unnecessary Hsp70 engagement. In all, our results provide a quantitative framework for understanding how client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic properties shape chaperone activity and show that the Hsp70 chaperone system does not altogether prevent aggregation: it merely retards it.

papers.title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.

papers.title: Mechanical Fidelity of Fixed-Cell Traction Force Microscopy
papers.abstract: Cellular traction forces contribute to biological processes including cell migration and tissue morphogenesis. Traction force microscopy (TFM) is widely used to quantify these forces in living cells, but it remains unclear how well measurements after fixation reproduce the live-cell state. Here, we systematically evaluated fixation-induced changes by paired comparison of the same cells before and after fixation using different fixation protocols and substrate stiffnesses. Fixation largely preserved the spatial organization and direction of substrate displacements and reconstructed traction fields, whereas displacement, traction, and strain-energy magnitudes showed fixation-dependent changes. Among the protocols tested, glutaraldehyde (GA) provided the closest agreement with live-cell measurements, retaining up to 99% of displacement and traction magnitudes and strain energy. Paraformaldehyde-based protocols caused larger reductions in these quantities while largely preserving their spatial organization. These results show that fixed-cell TFM, particularly with GA fixation under the conditions tested here, can provide measurements close to the live-cell state and offers a practical approach for combining TFM with post-fixation fluorescence imaging in a multi-well workflow.

papers.title: Lateral Membrane Heterogeneity Shapes Antimicrobial Association and Convergent Mechanical Responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are laterally heterogeneous, creating local physicochemical environments that can shape interactions with membrane-active antimicrobials. However, whether this spatial organization only affects local drug association or propagates into collective membrane responses remains unclear. Here we show that lateral membrane heterogeneity shapes antimicrobial association while distinct molecular responses converge on a common loss of membrane mechanical stability. Combining coarse-grained molecular dynamics, giant unilamellar vesicle fluctuation spectroscopy and microfluidic trapping, we follow octenidine, chlorhexidine and polymyxin B from molecular association to vesicle-scale behaviour. All three compounds preferentially associate with domain-associated membrane environments, but differ in how this preference changes with loading and in their effects on lipid mobility. Despite these differences, all three shift the membrane toward a mechanically softer state, while increasing exposure accelerates loss of vesicle stability under flow. These findings identify lateral membrane heterogeneity as an active determinant of antimicrobial response and provide a physical framework for understanding membrane-targeting activity beyond bulk composition and membrane-averaged charge.
